subsection: 5. Women in the workforce and equality legislation

notes.h: Why more women are in the workforce
notes.b: The share of women in paid work has risen steeply since the early 20th century, and the number of married women in work is far higher than in the past. Women's participation in paid work now forms a large part of the workforce. Several changes in education, family life, the economy and the law together explain this.
points: Education: more girls complete second level and third level, which gives them the qualifications for professional and managerial posts and raises their expectations of a career.
Contraception, smaller families and later marriage: women can plan when to have children and return to work after childbirth, or stay in employment, and they have fewer years of child rearing.

Economic need: the cost of housing, mortgages, rent and education means many families need two incomes, and some couples want a higher standard of living. Lone parents must earn because there is no second income.

Changing attitudes: work outside the home is now accepted for married women and mothers, equal opportunity is expected, and financial independence, job satisfaction and a career valued for its own sake are goals in themselves.

Equality legislation removed barriers: equal pay and equal treatment laws, and maternity leave with protection from dismissal. The marriage bar (the rule that women had to leave public-service jobs on marriage) was removed in 1973.

Childcare and supports: creches, childminders, pre-school and after-school services, and the free pre-school programme make it possible for parents to work outside the home. The National Childcare Scheme subsidises the costs.

Flexible work: part-time work, job-sharing, flexitime, term-time working and remote working help women combine work and family. The Work Life Balance and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 2023 gives a right to request flexible working.

Labour-saving appliances and convenience foods cut housework time, and the service sector grew, with more jobs in offices, health and education that suit women. Jobs have also become less gender-specific: women work as engineers, doctors and lawyers, and men work as nurses and childminders.
notes.tip: Examiners ask for three or four reasons, each explained, so name the factor and then say how it lets women work. Good choices are education, contraception and smaller families, economic need, changing attitudes, equality legislation, childcare, flexible work and labour-saving devices. Do not quote participation percentages.

notes.h: Effects of women's employment on family life
notes.b: When women move into paid work, the way a household earns money, shares tasks and cares for children changes. Examiners expect both the gains and the pressures, and a few effects reach beyond the family to society.
points: Dual-earner households (where both partners are in paid work) often have higher household incomes and a higher standard of living, and there is more security if one partner loses a job.
Women gain financial independence and self-esteem, so economic independence also gives them more choice about whether to remain in an unhappy marriage.
Women's employment has changed the division of housework and childcare, so many couples now share these tasks more equally and children see equal roles.

Combining a paid job with most of the housework and childcare creates role overload (too many roles to manage) and time pressure, especially for lone parents and parents of young children. This brings stress, tiredness and sometimes tension about sharing tasks.

The need for childcare means many families rely on grandparents, relatives or paid childminders, and childcare costs are a major expense. Children may be in care for long hours, and there is less time with children and less family time together.
Career moves can require relocation, so women's jobs can influence family decisions about where to live.
Effects on society: a bigger labour force and more tax revenue, smaller families, and more demand for childcare, convenience foods and services.
notes.tip: For a discussion of the impact on family life, cover income, shared tasks, role overload, childcare, independence and effects on children. At Higher Level, show the cause first (why more women work) and then the effect on the family.

notes.h: Equality legislation: equal pay and employment opportunities
notes.b: Laws exist so that women are not paid less or held back at work because of their gender. In Ireland the main law is the Employment Equality Acts 1998 to 2015, which cover every stage of employment.
points: The Employment Equality Acts 1998 to 2015 prohibit discrimination in employment on nine grounds: gender, civil status, family status, sexual orientation, religion, age, disability, race, and membership of the Traveller community.

They cover recruitment and advertising, access to training and promotion, pay, terms and conditions of work, harassment and dismissal. This means women and men have equal access to benefits linked to work.
Equal pay: men and women must receive equal pay for like work, meaning work that is the same, similar, or of equal value. An employee may claim equal pay on any of the nine grounds.
Equal opportunity: employers cannot refuse to hire, train or promote because of gender or marital status. An exception exists where a gender is a genuine occupational requirement.
Family status ground: this protects employees who are parents of children under 18, or carers of a person with a disability who needs care, against discrimination.

Pregnancy and maternity: the Maternity Protection Acts 1994 and 2004 give the right to maternity leave and protection against dismissal and loss of rights. Dismissal because of pregnancy is unlawful and is also treated as gender discrimination.
Maternity leave is a right to time off with job protection. Maternity benefit, the payment during leave, is a social insurance payment from the State, in most cases not from the employer.
Enforcement: complaints are made to the Workplace Relations Commission, with appeals to the Labour Court. The Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission promotes equality and can assist.
notes.tip: Equal pay means the same pay for like work, not the same pay for all jobs. Equal opportunity covers recruitment, training and promotion, not just pay. If asked to name and explain the legislation, give the Employment Equality Acts, equal pay for like work, the nine grounds and how a complaint is made.

notes.h: Related laws: gender pay gap reporting and equal status
notes.b: Two further laws sit alongside the Employment Equality Acts. One makes pay differences visible and the other covers areas outside the workplace, so it is important to know which law applies where.
points: The Gender Pay Gap Information Act 2021 requires larger employers to report the difference between men's and women's average hourly pay and to explain the gap. The size of employer covered has been widened in stages.
The Equal Status Acts 2000 to 2018 cover discrimination in goods, services and education, not employment, which is why employment complaints rely on the Employment Equality Acts.
notes.tip: Do not mix these up: the Equal Status Acts do not cover employment; the Employment Equality Acts do.

notes.b: Equality laws have opened the workplace, but women and men still do not have the same experience of work. Higher Level answers need to show what still holds women back.
points: Women are more likely than men to work part-time, often because of caring duties.
A gender pay gap persists in many sectors, partly because women and men are concentrated in different jobs.
Women are under-represented in senior management, a pattern known as the glass ceiling (an invisible barrier that stops women reaching the top posts).
Career breaks for childcare reduce pension entitlements and promotion chances, because time out means fewer years of contributions and less experience.
Affordable childcare is hard to find, and women still do most unpaid housework and caring, which limits the hours and posts they can take on.
notes.tip: Do not write that equality has been achieved. Higher Level answers on women's participation need the remaining barriers as well as the reasons for the rise.

notes.b: Women's working lives have changed greatly, and the best way to see this is to compare the past with today.
points: Compare women's employment and options a hundred years ago with today, for example the marriage bar and the range of jobs open.
Interview an older woman about her working life, and whether she left work on marriage.

keyTerms.definition: The proportion of the working-age population that is either in paid employment or actively seeking work.
A household in which both partners are in paid employment.
The principle that men and women are paid the same for the same work or work of equal value.
An arrangement in which two people share one full-time job and divide its hours, pay and responsibilities.
An arrangement that allows an employee to work during school terms and take unpaid leave during school holidays.
The concentration of men and women in different types of work, which can limit pay and promotion.
The difference between average pay for men and average pay for women in the labour market or a workplace.
Pressure that arises when a person faces too many demands from work and family responsibilities at once.
An invisible barrier that prevents qualified women from reaching senior management positions.

factCards.term: Four flexible working arrangements that help women combine work and family
factCards.definition: Part-time work, job-sharing, flexitime and term-time working.

factCards.term: Three areas covered by equality legislation at work
factCards.definition: Equal pay, equal treatment in recruitment and promotion, and equal terms and conditions of employment.

factCards.term: Three effects of women's employment on family life
factCards.definition: Higher household income, shared housework and childcare, and greater demand for childcare services.

factCards.term: Two reasons more women entered paid work
factCards.definition: Higher educational attainment and the economic need for a second income.

questions.prompt: Give two reasons why more women have entered the Irish workforce in recent decades.
questions.model: Higher educational attainment among women and their wish to use their qualifications. Economic need for a second income. Smaller families and access to contraception. Part-time and flexible working options that allow women to combine work and family.

questions.prompt: Analyse the effects of women's increased participation in paid work on family life, and explain how equal pay legislation supports women in employment.
questions.model: Effects: dual-earner households have higher incomes and greater financial independence for each partner, which can improve living standards and reduce dependence in marriage. Shared housework and childcare have become more common, but role overload and time pressure are a risk for parents, especially lone parents. Families depend more on childcare services, grandparents and relatives. Women's careers can shape decisions about where the family lives. Equal pay legislation: it requires employers to pay men and women the same for the same work or work of equal value. Equal opportunities rules prohibit discrimination in recruitment, promotion and training on grounds including gender and marital status. Employment rights protect women during pregnancy and maternity leave. These protections encourage women to stay in and return to paid work, although gender pay gaps and occupational segregation persist.
